events.title: First 3 install clients
events.decision: Which channel lands the first 3 paid $2,000 installs by Nov 30.
events.brief: A solo AI consultant at about $15k a month wants 3 paid $2,000 plugin installs by Nov 30 on 10 hours a week, with no email list. They lean toward direct outreach to 20 consultants.

hormozi.reason: Three sales is a lead and closing problem

garyvee.reason: Option A is a content and attention bet

martell.reason: 10 hours a week is the constraint

buffett.reason: Downside of the split and the $5k

welsh.reason: Solo, content-led selling, no audience yet

events.text:
SEAT: HORMOZI (Offers, pricing, and sales)
STANCE: Strong yes
OPTION SCORES: A 3/10 · B 9/10 · C 5/10 · D 1/10
PILLAR SCORE: 7/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: B, but bigger: message all 20 warm contacts this week with a done-for-you offer and a service guarantee, and ask every one of them for two names whether they buy or not.

WHY:
1. The constraint is leads, and warm outreach is the cheapest of the Core Four. D isn't a channel at all: "if you're not spending your day doing one of those core four things, you are not advertising." (Core Four, S070). Polishing with zero sales is hiding.
2. Let's do the math. I'm assuming 20 contacts, 50% reply, 10 calls, and a 30% close, which gets you 3 sales. That's a list with no slack. Two names from each person adds 40 warm-ish leads, and the same rates on those give you about 6 more. "Referrals are both worth worth more and cost less, which is a dangerous combo for making money as a business." (Lead getters, S112). Cash CAC is about $0, so even small numbers clear 3 to 1 easily.
3. C sounds like leverage, and partners are nodes (Lead getters, S112). But an agency owner won't push an offer with zero installs and zero proof. Get 3 case studies first and C scores 8 next month. A at under 2,000 followers can't reach the volume to judge in 30 days (Rule of 100, S002).

THE RISK I SEE: $2,000 is underpriced. Say install plus 30 days of tuning takes 15 hours. At your $15k-a-month consulting rate that's real cost, and you're well under 5 to 10x delivery (S094). If three installs eat your consulting hours, you've traded a good business for a worse one.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: Fewer than 5 of the 20 replying in 7 days. Then the offer is the problem, not the channel, and I'd rebuild it before touching anything else (Grand Slam Offer, S043).

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: Send 20 personal messages offering the install with a guarantee: if the feed doesn't give them usable ideas in 30 days, you keep tuning until it does (Guarantees, S026). Book calls and run them with questions, not demos (CLOSER, S069).

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: How many hours does one install plus 30 days of tuning actually take you?

events.name: Alex Hormozi

events.text:
SEAT: GARY V (Marketing and attention)
STANCE: Yes
OPTION SCORES: A 6/10 · B 8/10 · C 4/10 · D 1/10
PILLAR SCORE: 7/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: B is the right hook and A is the jabs. Message the 20 consultants this week, and post every install on LinkedIn every day while you do it.

WHY:
1. Day Trading Attention (S096). The cheapest attention you own is the 20 people who already trust you. It costs nothing and you can sell to it today. Running the math on assumptions: 20 messages, about 6 calls, a 35% close rate, and you get 2 installs. That's good, but it's not 3. It's short by one.
2. LinkedIn is where that gap closes. My 2026 call still stands: "You own LinkedIn and you don't do it." (S043, 2026). Under 2,000 followers doesn't matter: "Because we live in interest media, not social media, you do not need followers to get views." (S043, 2026). Do 30 posts at an assumed 400 views each. That's 12,000 views from consultants and agency people, and it only has to produce 3 or 4 warm DMs to land install number three.
3. "Document. Don't create." (S143, 2016). Your product literally generates content ideas, my friends. Run it on yourself. Screen-record the feed for each prospect's niche and post each install's before and after. That takes 30 minutes a day, not a separate shoot. C pays out $600 a deal through partners you haven't tested, and D buys nothing. "Cash is what allows you to do everything else. Cash is oxygen." (S128, 2015).

THE RISK I SEE: You spend the 10 hours polishing posts and never book the calls. Content is the side dish this month and outreach is the steak. Cap content at 3 hours a week.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: If the 20 messages produce fewer than 5 calls by November 9, the offer is the problem, not the channel. Then I'd fix the offer before spending one more hour on content.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: By Monday, November 2, send 20 personal messages, each with a 60-second screen recording of the plugin's feed built for that person's niche. Post the first one on LinkedIn today.

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: Will you actually post on LinkedIn every day for 30 days, or do you hate it? If you hate it, I want to know now so we cut A to zero and go all in on B.

events.text:
SEAT: WELSH (Solo business and content-led growth)
STANCE: Yes (on B, with a thin content lane alongside)
OPTION SCORES: A 4/10 · B 8/10 · C 3/10 · D 1/10
PILLAR SCORE: 6/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: Run B now with a scrappy offer, and post once a week about each install so the next 3 clients come from content, not favors.

WHY:
1. My own lens misfires here, so I'll say it plainly. Under 2,000 followers, no list, 30 days. If daily posts reach about 1,500 people each, I'd expect a handful of DMs and maybe zero $2,000 buyers by Nov 30. Audience-first works, but it takes months, not weeks (S047, S064). A is the right engine for Q1. It is the wrong engine for this deadline.
2. B is the easy version. "Instead, find out whether the simplest version works first." (S004) It needs one page with the price and scope, a short DM, and a calendar link. 20 messages, maybe 10 replies, 6 calls, 3 closes. A 15% close rate from a warm network is realistic. And ask clearly: "One of the key mistakes I see solopreneurs making is their hesitancy to ask for the business." (S083)
3. C makes the business harder to run. Two partners, $600 off every sale, and their clients' custom requests landing on you. "It couldn’t make the business harder to run." (S004) D is polishing with no buyer to tell you what to polish: "today’s scrappy version beats the polished version you're waiting for." (S040)

THE RISK I SEE: The win. Three installs plus 30 days of tuning each could take about 30 of your 40 hours this month, before any selling. "An opportunity can work exactly as promised and give you a business you don’t want to run." (S007) Cap it at 3 and do not take a fourth until December.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: If fewer than 5 of the 20 reply within 7 days, the network is too cold. Then I'd move hours into A and give it 90 days.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: Write the one-page offer, then send all 20 DMs by Friday, each with a clear price and a "want in?" ask.

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: How many hours does one install plus 30 days of tuning really take, and does 3 of them fit inside your 10 hours a week?

events.name: Justin Welsh

events.text:
SEAT: GRAHAM (Product and startups)
STANCE: Strong yes
OPTION SCORES: A 3/10 · B 9/10 · C 3/10 · D 1/10
PILLAR SCORE: 7/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: B, but run it as a demand test. Talk to all 20 consultants one by one this week, and show each of them a feed built on their own competitors before you ask for $2,000.

WHY:
1. Nobody has bought this yet, so the only question that matters is whether anyone wants it. Twenty conversations answer that in two weeks. LinkedIn posts don't, and an agency partner doesn't either. Recruiting users yourself is the core of (Do things that don't scale, S096), and the scoring rule there is blunt: low if you are "waiting on a launch, a partnership, or a hire to bring users." A and C are both forms of waiting.
2. The arithmetic. 3 sales out of 20 needs a 15% close rate. That's high for strangers and reasonable for warm contacts, if the pain is real. Assume 2 hours per contact for outreach, a call and a custom demo feed. That's 40 hours, which is exactly 4 weeks at 10 hours a week. A with under 2,000 followers (assumed) can't get there in 30 days. C gives away $600 a sale to partners who have never sold this and have no reason to push it yet. "Partnerships too usually don't work." (S096)
3. D is the classic mistake. "Launching too slowly has probably killed a hundred times more startups than launching too fast" (S178). The first three buyers will show you what to polish.
4. A concession: this is a services offer, not a startup, so the growth reflex fits it less well. But with $15k a month coming in, the founder is default alive either way and the $5k never gets touched (S080). So the only real risk here is wasted time.

THE RISK I SEE: Friends say yes to be kind. Three polite payments from your own network prove loyalty, not demand, and then the 4th sale never happens.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: Fewer than 5 of the 20 agreeing to a call in week one, or nobody asking an unprompted follow-up question after seeing their own feed. Either would mean the pain isn't sharp enough, and I'd stop selling installs and go find out why.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: Build a sample feed for the 5 warmest contacts, using their real competitors, and send each one personally with the price stated.

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: Which of the 20 is losing money or sleep right now because they don't know what to post, and how do you know?

events.text:
SEAT: MARTELL (People, hiring, and founder time)
STANCE: Yes
OPTION SCORES: A 3/10 · B 8/10 · C 5/10 · D 1/10
PILLAR SCORE: 7/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: Go with B, and record the first install on camera so installs two and three take half the founder hours.

WHY:
1. Buyback Rate (S018). $15k a month is $180k a year. Divide by 2,000 hours and you get $90 an hour, so the Buyback Rate is $22.50. This window is 10 hours a week for 30 days, about 43 hours, so that is the budget. B costs about 10 of them: 20 personal messages at 15 minutes each is 5 hours, plus about 8 calls at 30 minutes each is 4 hours. A costs 5 to 7 hours every week for daily posts to under 2,000 followers. That uses most of the budget before anyone has paid.
2. Replacement Ladder (S031). Sales is rung four. "Sales is four because you as a CEO will always be able to sell better than anybody else you hire." The offer is new and nobody has bought it yet, so the founder sells it by hand. With C, partners are pitching an offer with no proof behind it.
3. Camcorder Method (S020). The real calendar risk is delivery, not sales. I'm assuming 10 hours per install plus 30 days of tuning, so 3 clients is about 30 hours. Add 10 hours of selling and you're at 40 of the 43. "I use this thing called the camcorder method I literally record myself doing the work while I'm doing the work so it takes me no extra time." Stagger the start dates. Once the second install is done, partners have proof to sell with. That's when C fits: "That's what a partner does and it is the most powerful way to get customers." (S036)

THE RISK I SEE: All three say yes in week one. Thirty hours of delivery lands on top of $15k a month of consulting, and the consulting clients pay for it.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: If one install plus tuning takes more than 15 founder hours, three won't fit in 43. I'd cap it at two or raise the price.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: Send all 20 messages by Friday and offer staggered start dates: week 1, week 2, week 3.

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: How many hours does one install actually take you, start to finish? D is the Staller time assassin (S059), so don't hide behind polishing. Know that number before you sell.

events.name: Dan Martell

events.text:
SEAT: BUFFETT (Money and capital)
STANCE: Yes
OPTION SCORES: A 4/10 · B 8/10 · C 6/10 · D 2/10
PILLAR SCORE: 9/10
CONFIDENCE: 4/5
RUIN RISK: none
DOOR: two-way

THE CALL: Option B. Send 20 personal notes this week, keep the $5k reserve untouched, and add C as a pay-only-on-collected-cash backup if B lands fewer than two by mid-November.

WHY:
1. Birds in the bush (S011). B costs no cash, only hours. I'm assuming each install plus 30 days of tuning takes about 12 hours and selling takes 4 more. That works out to $2,000 over 16 hours, about $125 an hour. Your consulting runs about $94 an hour (I'm assuming $15k over 160 hours). That beats it, and the money comes back inside 30 days.
2. Cost of capital is the second-best idea (S013): "is what could be produced by our second best idea. And then our best idea has to exceed that." Under C you keep $1,400 a sale, about $88 an hour on the same hours, which trails your own consulting. C is fine as a backup channel. It shouldn't be the first swing. A is slow and D brings in nothing.
3. Great, good, and gruesome (S080), my translation to a service offer: no new capital goes in, so the only way this turns gruesome is if "30 days of tuning" quietly turns into 30 hours of tuning. You can't make a margin back once you've given it away.
4. Where my lens misfires: this is building from zero (S051). So I won't ask for proven earning power before you swing. Waiting under D is a mistake of omission (S028), and you never see that kind of mistake on the books.

THE RISK I SEE: You'd be selling an unproven product to the 20 people whose good opinion you most need. If the install flops, the money is small but the network is not. "We can afford to lose money but we can't afford to lose reputation." (S028)

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: If the first install takes more than 20 hours, it pays less than your consulting and I'd reprice before selling the next one. If an agency partner shows me 50 or more qualified buyers, C moves up.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK: Write a one-page scope with a capped tuning allowance and a full-refund guarantee. Then send the 20 notes.

QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER: How many hours did your own install and first month of tuning actually take?

events.text:
SEAT: HORMOZI
I DISAGREE MOST WITH: Graham. His line: C is a form of waiting, because "Partnerships too usually don't work." (S096). My rebuttal: partners add nodes, and nodes beat leads. "You've got customers, employees, agencies, and affiliates, and lead getters using the core 4 complete the advertising cycle." (Lead getters, S112). Here's the full-strength case for C. Two agency owners with maybe 30 clients each gives you 60 qualified buyers, against 20 favors. Those buyers are strangers to you, so C is the one option that answers Graham's own loyalty worry. Cash CAC is $600, paid only when a sale closes, against $2,000. That math works.

I CONCEDE: Welsh and Martell are right that delivery hours, not leads, are the real constraint. That is the weak spot in my C case. If 20 warm contacts get you 3 sales, a partner's 4th lead is a sale you can't deliver. So C survives as a pipeline you open this week. It does not replace B.

ON THE CRUXES:
1. Start C now, but small: two 30-minute calls, each with a demo feed built on the agency's own competitors. No referral launch until install 1 is done.
2. At 15 hours each, three installs don't fit. The 30-day tuning spills into December, though, so only selling and setup land inside the 43 hours. Cap tuning at 4 hours in writing.
3. Paid at full price with no discount, a yes is cash. It isn't proof. Proof is whether they hand you names. Ask every buyer for two.

SEAT: GARY V
I DISAGREE MOST WITH: Graham. His argument: three payments from friends prove loyalty, not demand. I agree with the diagnosis and reject the fix. If you only sell inside the 20, you never get a demand test, because the 20 are not a market. Strangers are the test, and the cheapest way to reach them is interest media: "you do not need followers to get views." (S043, 2026). A DM from a stranger who saw an install post is the demand proof Graham wants. Friends pay the bills this month. Strangers tell you if there's a business.

I CONCEDE: Martell's hours math. 43 hours, minus 10 for selling, minus about 30 for delivery, leaves 3. My Round 1 cap of 3 hours a week of content adds up to about 13 hours, and that doesn't fit. Daily posting is out. What changes is that content has to come out of delivery, not out of extra hours. Martell already gave us how: record the install while you do it (his Camcorder Method).

ON THE CRUXES:
1. No partner deal before proof. Make the install posts so good the agency owners see them, and then sign C in December with two case studies in hand.
2. Daily posting doesn't fit. Three posts a week does, cut from the install recordings, about 1 hour a week. "Document. Don't create." (S143, 2016).
3. Warm yeses prove the offer can close, not that there's demand. Real demand is one buyer from outside the network.

I DISAGREE MOST WITH: the partner case for C now (Chair's steelman, backed by Hormozi S112 and Martell S036). Their line: two agency owners already have client lists and trust, so they reach more buyers than 20 favors.
I once turned down guaranteed partner revenue because of the extra work and Slack noise. Same rule applies here. "It couldn’t make the business harder to run." Partnerships come in my growth phase, after Stay Alive and Build Systems (S068). My better move is to pitch those two agency owners as buyers. Small agencies are the target market. Once they have bought, ask them to refer (S082).

2. It fits with caps. Install 4 hours, tuning capped at 1 hour a week for 4 weeks, so 8 hours per client and 24 total. Add 10 hours of selling and that's 34 of the 43. Starts are staggered. If install 1 takes more than 10 hours, stop at 2.
3. No. A demand signal is one stranger's DM from the weekly install post, or one referral who isn't on the 20.

events.text:
SEAT: MARTELL

I DISAGREE MOST WITH: Graham. His line is that partners are just "waiting" on someone else to bring users. Here is C at full strength. A partner costs zero founder selling hours. You pay only on collected cash, and 30% is the fair-feeling split (S063). Partners with non-competing audiences are "the most powerful way to get customers." (S036). And a partner's client is a stranger, so one partner sale is the only real demand test on the table. Does it survive this week? No. The calendar kills it, not the logic. Sales is rung four on the Replacement Ladder (S020), and right now nobody can sell this better than you. Two agency owners pitching an unrecorded install means you hand off with no playbook and no way to check the work. That is the Procter and Gamble story, about $500K lost to a handoff nobody monitored (S103). So C survives as one partner call, after install one is on camera.

I CONCEDE: Hormozi and Buffett on hours. If an install takes 15 to 20 hours, three installs are 45 to 60 hours. Add 10 hours of selling and you're at 55 to 70 against a 43-hour budget. That changes my cap. Sell two starts in November, and the third only if install one comes in under 12 hours.

ON THE CRUXES:
1. Partners: one call, after proof. Not two partners signed this week.
2. At 15 to 20 hours, the overflow of 12 to 27 hours comes out of consulting. At my $90 an hour (S018), that costs $1,080 to $2,430. Price that in or raise the price.
3. Warm yeses prove you can close. They don't prove demand. Two things do: a referral to a stranger, or a partner sale.

SEAT: BUFFETT
I DISAGREE MOST WITH: Martell. His line: three installs at 10 hours each plus 10 hours of selling fit in 43 hours. That's 40 of 43, so the cushion is 3 hours, and it rests on a number nobody has measured. Graham budgets 2 hours per contact, which is 40 hours of selling alone. Add three installs at my 12 hours and you're at 76 hours against a 43-hour budget. I don't swing without a margin of safety (Price is what you pay, S086), and this plan has none. Stagger the starts and log the hours on install one before promising anyone a third start date.

I CONCEDE: Hormozi on price. At my old 20-hour line, $2,000 pays $100 an hour, and my consulting pays about $94. That's no margin at all, and I should have caught it. I'm lowering my repricing line to 15 hours. These three sell as a stated founding price, and the fourth is quoted at $3,000 or more.

ON THE CRUXES:
1. Sign the partners now, but they start selling only after install one ships. Paying them only out of collected cash keeps the cash risk at zero, so my backup stands. The real cost is hours, and a partner's client who gets a flop costs two reputations, not one.
2. Three only fit if install plus tuning comes in under 12 hours. Otherwise cap it at two this month.
3. Graham is right. Charge full price with no discount and a full-refund guarantee, which protects the network. Demand is proven only when someone outside the 20 pays. "We can afford to lose money but we can't afford to lose reputation." (S028)
